blocks.content: Building on the embeddings API, fine-tuning APIs cover the practical mechanism

2. Uploading Training Data

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A training data file gets uploaded to the provider

blocks.text: This connects directly to dataset preparation, covered extensively in the separate Fine-Tuning course, before creating a fine-tuning job, your prepared training data needs to be uploaded as a file through a dedicated files endpoint, receiving back a file identifier used in the next step.
3. Creating a Fine-Tuning Job

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: An uploaded file ID gets used to create a fine-tuning job

blocks.text: With the training file uploaded, creating a fine-tuning job specifies the uploaded file identifier and the base model to fine-tune, this connects directly to supervised fine-tuning, covered in the separate Fine-Tuning course, the underlying training process itself.
4. Monitoring Job Status

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A job status moves from queued to running to succeeded

blocks.text: A fine-tuning job progresses through several status stages, checking status periodically, or waiting for a completion notification if the platform supports one, lets your application know exactly when the resulting fine-tuned model is actually ready to use.

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A fine-tuned model ID gets used directly in a Chat Completions call

blocks.text: This connects directly to Chat Completions, covered earlier in this module, once a fine-tuning job succeeds, it produces a specific model identifier for your new fine-tuned model, used exactly like any standard model identifier in a normal chat completion request.
6. Cost and Time Considerations

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Training cost and inference cost afterward are both worth tracking

blocks.text: Fine-tuning carries two distinct cost components, the training process itself, and ongoing usage of the resulting fine-tuned model afterward, this connects directly to the cost optimization concepts covered elsewhere in this course, both need to be weighed against the actual benefit fine-tuning provides for your specific use case.

blocks.title: This connects directly to the broader fine-tuning versus prompt engineering tradeoff
blocks.content: The earlier Why Prompt Engineering Matters topic covered this same underlying tradeoff, fine-tuning genuinely costs more in time and money than prompt engineering alone, worth reserving for cases where prompt engineering has genuinely been exhausted first.

blocks.text: 7. Required Training Data Format

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Training data must follow a required JSONL format, with each line one training example

blocks.text: This connects directly to JSON payloads, covered in an earlier module, training data needs to follow a specific JSONL format, one JSON object per line, each representing one training example, exactly matching the message structure covered in the earlier Chat Completions topic, getting this format right is a genuine prerequisite before uploading.
8. A Worked Fine-Tuning API Example

A team fine-tuning a model for a specific customer support tone uploads their prepared JSONL training file, creates a fine-tuning job specifying the base model, monitors the status until it reaches succeeded, and then uses the resulting fine-tuned model identifier directly in their production Chat Completions calls.
9. Fine-Tuning APIs vs the Separate Fine-Tuning Course

This topic covers the concrete, mechanical steps of this provider specific fine-tuning API, the separate Fine-Tuning course covers the much deeper conceptual foundation, why and when to fine-tune, dataset preparation, training techniques, and evaluation, both are genuinely necessary for successfully fine-tuning a model in practice.
Worked Example

A developer new to fine-tuning initially uploads a training file with a subtly incorrect JSONL format, missing a required field in one example, the fine-tuning job fails immediately with a validation error rather than proceeding with corrupted data.

Correcting the training data format to match the exact required structure, and re-uploading before creating the job again, resolves the issue, demonstrating why validating training data format carefully before uploading saves a wasted, failed job attempt.
Common Mistakes

items: Uploading training data with an incorrect JSONL format, causing the fine-tuning job to fail validation
Not monitoring job status and missing when a fine-tuned model actually becomes ready to use
Reaching for fine-tuning before genuinely exhausting what prompt engineering alone could achieve
Not accounting for both training cost and ongoing inference cost when budgeting for a fine-tuning project

blocks.text: Practice

Prepare a small sample training dataset in the required JSONL format for a task you are familiar with, and sketch out the sequence of API calls, uploading the file, creating the job, checking status, and using the resulting model, needed to actually run this fine-tuning process.
Key Takeaway

OpenAI fine-tuning API involves uploading a correctly formatted training data file, creating a fine-tuning job against a base model, monitoring its status until it succeeds, and then using the resulting fine-tuned model identifier directly in standard chat completion calls, this concrete workflow is the practical mechanism behind the much deeper fine-tuning concepts covered in the separate Fine-Tuning course.
